analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Cases submitted, we'll hear arguments next in 1844, city of Mobile against Bolden and the consolidated case. Side wine there's yeah buying convinced 적 appli inspires Thank you. I think we may proceed now, whenever you're ready, Mr. Ryan. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. The issue in the case that I present to you is whether Mobile's election system, under which it elects its commissioners in at-large elections, is constitutional. Now, Mobile is a city of 190,000 people. One-third of them are black. There has never been a black commissioner elected. And I think that the ultimate issue that is presented to this Court in this case is whether or not these blacks, who are the plaintiffs in this case, are deprived of the equal protection of the laws. Are they deprived of equal access and equal participation in the election system of Mobile, as they allege in their complaint? Can you tell me, Mr. Ryan, I know that commissioner form of municipal government is a very common one, but it's one with which I have only a passing familiarity. All righty. Commissioners have both executive and legislative powers? Yes, they do. That's really the big distinction between the commission form of government and, say, the mayor of council. Each commissioner is elected as the finance commissioner, the safety commissioner, or the public's works commissioner. Well, that specialization has been true only fairly recently. The commission form of government, as I remember from reading the briefs, again, in Mobile in 1911, was it? Yes, it did. And the specialization, at least officially, the specialization is more recent, isn't it? I believe that, as a matter of fact, the specialization, insofar as prescribed by law, was laid out in 1965. Right. But, Mr. Justice Stewart, I think it has always been a factor of specialization. Yes. Anyone who ran for the commission, say, I'm running for the finance post because I'm an expert in finance. I'm running for the police or safety post because I'm an expert in police. Or I'm running for the public works department because I am an expert in that. I guess the big difference between the commission form, which is more like the city manager form than any other claim. Well, it is unlike it, too. It is. But am I then correct in understanding that all of the legislative power and all of the executive power of the municipality reside in these three commissioners? That is true. That is true. All of both powers. All of the powers. The city manager form of government. Of course, the city manager is exclusively an executive. Yes, that's right. And the council is the legislature. That is right. And when I was saying that when they do the administrative or executive work, they're more like city managers. But they also enact the ordinances, do they? They also enact the ordinances. But the people know which of the three are responsible for each of the functions of the city. And as of necessity, this form of government, which began around the turn of the century, was elected to wipe out the corruption mayor-alderman form that was causing a lot of problems at that time. And it gives each commissioner absolute responsibility to each voter. Mr. R. You've just explained that the people run on a place basis here in Mobile. Now, it seems to me that I grew up in a place where we had the commission form of government, but each one was appointed by the mayor to the public works or public safety or what it was. But here, the candidates run for a specific position. Yes, Your Honor. That's true. I think one of the really great things about the field of municipal government, and I've been in it since 1937, is every city is different when you come right down to it. You can't say that one city is precisely like another. I don't care how you go about it and how you describe it. But isn't there a common denominator in terms of having them exercise, as Mr. Justice Stewart suggested, both executive and legislative functions? Yes. That's the common denominator of the commission form, isn't it? Yes, it is. And they have to adopt the policies and then carry them out. But I think the major thing is that the people know, when they vote for them, that they're voting for this man because he's an expert in finance, and this man, he's an expert in police safety, and this man because he is an expert in public works. And regardless of whether or not they run as such, as they did not prior to 1965, it was always understood this man was running for this post and that man was running for that post. May I ask another question? Do they run as a trio on a ticket? I know it's a nonpartisan election, at least that's my understanding. That's right. It is a nonpartisan election. First of all, what is the term of a commissioner? Four years. And are they all elected at the same time? Yes, they are. And do they run as a slate of three? No. No. There is no primary. It's a nonpartisan election. And there are no impediments to anybody registering, anybody qualifying to be a candidate for any one of the places, even though they're not an expert in finance or an expert in one of the others. And there's no question but what. There's equal participation in the electoral process and that the votes are counted equally. And have Negroes been? They have run. Yes. Now, Negroes have run. Three Negroes ran in 1973. They ran or they stood for election? Mr. Justice Marshall, I would say in the South they stood for election. Yes, sir. And you're right. They stood for election in 1973. But as the district court pointed out, they were young, inexperienced, and ran rather limited campaigns and didn't even care of the black wards. Yes, sir. Now, that... Is there some prerequisites for getting on the ballot? None whatever. There isn't a filing fee? I suppose sometimes... There was a minor filing... But there's not a signature requirement. There must be. Now, Mr. Arendell is here. He's a great expert that tried to make an expert out of me, but I'm saying there isn't... There is no signature requirement of any substance? No. Absolutely not. So anybody can run. Now, this is the first case that I know of that comes before this court that really squarely involves at-large elections in the municipal level. Well, Mr. Arendell, before you go on with that, you might just tell me why you thought it was important to say that these commissioners either formally or informally stood for election for certain positions. Yes. Now, let's just assume that they didn't. Would your case be different? Suppose they just ran. All they ran was for three commissioners, and no one ever knew what they were running for except they were running for commissioners, and they had the full legislative power. It might so happen that after they were elected, one would assume this kind of executive responsibility, and one would assume another. But suppose they just ran. When they ran, no one understood anything other than that they were running for three commissioners exercising legislative power. Would your case be different or not? That's a pretty hard question, but I would say that my case would not be different because in every commission form of government that I know of, the people always know who that commissioner is running for and who they're voting for. Now, you've had a lot of experience in Cincinnati with proportional representation in voting and such. But I say, coming back to my point, that this is the first case before this court involving at-large election. We have 67% of the cities. Well, I take that your case would be the same if there was just at-large election for a city councilman. I would agree, except I think here you have a special reason because the people can better hold these commissioners responsible for their actions because they know who takes the action. So you do want us to confine our decision to address the commission form of government, where you run for a spot? Yes. The city council, generally speaking, as a generality, has only legislative power. That is right. Not executive power. That is right. And you have a city manager. You have a mayor who runs the overall. I want to suggest to you that the commission form of government, as you described in Mobile, is certainly very different from the commission form of government as we knew it in New Jersey. My father was for 13 years a member of the city commission of Newark. And there you had as many as 80 candidates, and the first five were elected, and then the five of them, by majority vote, decided which should be director of public safety, which should be director of public affairs, and so forth. And one did not run because he was supposed to be an expert in any particular field. Now, you're speaking of a county, are you not? No, I am not. I'm speaking of the city of New York. We had the commission form of government in New Jersey for some 25 years, and most of the major cities have the commission form. Yes. Well. Well, that takes me back to my comments. I do welcome. It's the mayor. The mayor assignment. Who made the assignment of the places. So there are, as you pointed out, all variations. But I join Mr. Justice White in asking whether your case would be the same without a place contest standing for a place. Well, I think that on reconsideration, I would say we'll be the same. I think that the election at large is the important thing here. And it is true, though, that there is a tremendous battle about the qualifications of the various commissioners, because I, too, Mr. Justice Brennan, grew up in. My father ran in. And it's too long ago. I don't remember how many candidates. But this was county and not city. And so I think this... I think you indicated before that the distinguishing factor, perhaps, was that these people exercised both legislative and executive functions. That's right. And that's not different. That sort of distinguished it from... From the usual mayor or council, former government. That is very true. What about the police jury in Texas and Louisiana? The county police jury. Mr. Justice. He talked about everything that's different all over the world. Well, that's... That's right. And... The judge is a layman in Texas. And the judge is a layman... In the jury. In Missouri, where President Truman was. That's right. And a judge is a layman in Illinois. But let me get back to this fact. One of the most interesting things to me is that these plaintiffs have brought this suit. They have 35% black. But never has a qualified black run for office in Mobile. Now, if there's any one thing that this court can judicially notice, and Mr. Justice Marshall knows better than anybody else, that it's this. When I first started representing cities in 1937, there wasn't a single black that I know of on any city council and certainly no black mayor. Today we have a tremendous number. Mr. And how can you know whether a particular individual, black or white, is, quote, qualified, close quote? Well, he has to state his qualifications, and the people vote for him on the basis of his qualifications. He puts forth his qualifications in the race. Well, if I might be anecdotal, too, I grew up in Milwaukee. We had a city council of 23 members. Twelve of them were tavern keepers. Well, the city council of Milwaukee doesn't really run the city. The mayor, who was Mayor Holm probably then, and a city manager generally run the city. But the thing is that here you've got Mayor Bradley running out in Los Angeles in a city that's 17% black. He ran once, he was defeated. He ran the next time he's been elected. And he'd be elected over and over again. And I say around this nation, and we cite them on page 11 and 12 of our brief, good many illustrations. Raleigh, North Carolina, 22% black. Black mayor. Got a black mayor of Atlanta. Black mayor of New Orleans. Black mayor of Newark. Black mayor of Oakland. I could name 100 of them almost, because I work with them almost daily. And I'm saying that we've reached a point in our nation where the color of a man's skin in the political area doesn't count as much as his ability to prove that he can do the job. Well, why is it that he has a city in Mobile? I didn't quite hear... Are they all stupid in Mobile? Now, Mr. Justice Marshall, you probably knew John LaFleur very well. He's one of the ableist Americans who ever lived. I'm sorry, he was a plaintiff here. He's dead. Now, I would be awfully hard to convince that if John LaFleur ran with 35% black, that he wouldn't get enough white votes to win. And my statement to you is... He was a postal carrier. Pardon? He was a mail carrier. Well, he was a brilliant man. Well, he wasn't a politician. He was a mail carrier. Well, he's a politician, too, and you know it. Yeah, well, that's part-time politician. Well... Why is he named some of those young lawyers down in Mobile? He organized the only slating organization that existed in Mobile, the nonpartisan voters' leg, which is black. Well, if the qualification factor is relevant here at all... I think it's very relevant. The only evidence of qualification is that the three Negroes who ran, you said according to this record, did not carry the Negro... Wards. ...voting wards. Isn't that about all we can deal with on qualifications? Well, Your Honor, I think it shows the sophistication of the voters today. And I think it also shows that the voters are looking at the qualifications of the candidates rather than the color of their skin. Or they would have gotten 35% of the vote. The difficulty that in this case, though, I know you talk about the rest of the country, but in this case the district court's findings are, as I remember them, that the color of a man's skin is of critical importance in the election. Quote, the kiss of death, end quote. Don't we have to look at Mobile rather than Oakland and Cleveland and other places? Well, I read the kiss of death, Mr. Justice Marshall, and I read what the judge said about polarization. But do we accept those findings or do we not for purposes of our decision? I say that the findings are based on mighty thin evidence because the expert testified that polarization was lessening all the time. And there were witnesses who testified that a black man would have a reasonable opportunity to win. Do we accept those findings for purposes of our decision or do you ask us to reexamine them? I ask you to reexamine them because... Is it critical to your case that we reexamine them? Not particularly. I think that what you have here is a legal conclusion rather than a fact because what did the court do? In a voting rights case, you've got to find some barrier, some obstacle. Now, in Mobile, you have full access, full participation by blacks. Yes, but Mr. Justice Stevens points out that the district court said you may have complete access until the voters get into the voting booths. And then there's voting on the basis of color. And no black has ever been elected. Well, let's just assume that's so. That is true. Now, let's just assume that that is the... Just accept those findings. And you say... And you say... What do you say to that? I say to that that the evidence is that polarization is growing less and less all the time and that this court must pay some attention to the fact that blacks... Throughout the nation. What if we accept the findings that there is racial voting at the polls? Mr. Ryan, all your polarization is changing. What about the Klan getting 1,500 members a week in Alabama? The Ku Klux Klan I'm talking about. You know, KKK. Yeah, I'm heard of it. 1,500 members a week in Alabama in the last two months. I don't follow its activities quite as close, I'm afraid. Well, it seems to lose, baby. Well, I would say that the Ku Klux Klan, as far as I know of it, is fading as a factor in the South, just as polarization of the black vote is fading. I thought your argument, Mr. Ryan, was that even accepting polarization, nothing in either the 14th or 15th Amendment requires that this at-large form of election, which has been the form adopted by Mobile since the year 1911, to be altered. Well, my... Even accepting that Negroes vote as Negroes and white voters vote as white people. My position is... There's nothing in the Constitution, the 14th Amendment or the 15th Amendment or any other part of it, that requires Alabama to change its system of voting. That is right. I think as long as they have equal access and equal participation, and their votes are counted equally, that's all the Constitution requires. There's no one-man-one-vote problem here under the 14th Amendment. No, they're all equal. And there's no deprivation of anybody's voting under the 15th Amendment, based on his race or color. That is right, because testimony is this, that the black vote is decisive. All the candidates for commissioner campaigned very hard for the black vote. And on pages 141, 142, 143, you have Reverend Hope saying that he feels, he's head of the nonpartisan voters' league, he feels that the three white candidates, or three white commissioners who now occupy those offices, treat the blacks very well. And we have over and over again the fact that these commissioners have the open-door policy, they see the blacks, they try to take care of their problem. Sure, they can't take care of them all. All cities have problems. But... And, Mr. Ryan, did not the district court find that the blacks were not getting the same services from their government that the whites were? Isn't that the district court's finding? Well, the finding on services, there are other remedies for that, Mr. Justice Stevens. Well, I understand that. I'm not saying you necessarily lose your opinion. I've done everything with the voting. Don't we have to deal with the findings of the district court rather than changing conditions that you described that are taking place today? Or do we? Normally we deal with the findings the district court made, and we've got to live with them. I don't think you can decide this case in a vacuum. I think you have to look at the entirety of the picture of what's going on in the world today. I think that in this instance where there's no impediment in the voting process, whatever, everybody can register, everybody can run. Do you think the Gamaliel case would have been decided differently if there had been a showing that there was no impediment to the voting process? Well, the Gamaliel case is entirely different from this. The Gamaliel case was an out-and-out discriminatory action. We've got no discrimination here. Suppose this was out-and-out in the sense that the legislature and the commissioner said the reason we want to maintain our plan, our commission form of government, is because we do not want blacks to be elected as commissioners. Would it be a different case? It could be, but you don't have that here. You don't have any intentional discrimination. You have absolute equality of voters to the voting process. Based on the findings of the district court, at some point in the process, you have a deliberate discrimination in the voting booth. Well, I'm not suggesting that. Mr. Justice White, there's no such finding. What they... Well, I'll call it polarization then. Racial voting, whatever you want to call it. Well, even on that, I say that the testimony was, by the expert, voiled that polarization is lessening. And the government, in its brief, concedes that race was not an issue in the 1973 election, which was the last election. Now, what the court did, the district court did, was it couldn't find an obstacle, it couldn't find any impediment, and found that everybody had an unfettered right to vote. So what it did was, and I quote the court, the court concludes that an at-large system is an effective barrier to blacks seeking public life. Well, that simply isn't true. It simply isn't true. It does not. The record here is not the record here that the three Negro candidates didn't carry the Negro awards in conflict to some extent with the district court's finding. Absolutely. And then the court of appeals went a step further and said that that existence, that so-called barrier to blacks seeking public life establishes the element of intent. Now, I think that this case is enormously important because having found that the system itself was the barrier, all the court could do was abolish it. And what did they do? They wrote an entire new city chart with a mayor and nine city councilmen because they said that the only way, and I quote the district court again, that you can provide blacks with a realistic opportunity to elect blacks to the city governing body, is to wipe out the existing government and put in a mayor council plan with single-member districts. Now, I don't think this court's in the business of fixing elections or guaranteeing that a person is going to be able to vote and put in office a man of his own color. They have an equal right to an equal shot. One man, one vote. Mr. Ryan, I suppose it's only, it's just the residential pattern that would allow, that would afford the kind of a remedy the district court gave here. If blacks and whites were equally distributed around the city of Mobile, and yet the same results had occurred down in the past, there weren't any blacks elected, the only remedy would be a system of racial proportional representation. The single-member district remedy would only work because of residential patterns, I take it. I think the vicious part, you're right, the vicious part of this decision is that it more or less freezes segregation. You mean residential segregation? Yes. If you're going to chop up Mobile into nine single-member districts, and the blacks start moving out of the district, they lose control of it. So I think that's really, to me, we've reached a point, I say, when color shouldn't count. And it hasn't counted throughout the nation. And I think this court should say so, that you're not going to provide proportional representation by race. If you never have, decision after decision, you've said no, equal vote yes, equal access yes, equal participation yes, but not proportional representation by race. In fact, proportional representation, that is the hair system of proportional representation, has existed, I think, only in two municipalities in the United States, New York City for a while, and Cincinnati, Ohio for a longer period. And that was attacked as being unconstitutional at one stage. Yes. And it didn't work very well either place. Well, one can argue about that. All right, but Morris, he's the dude who put it in in Cincinnati, told me it wasn't working very good, and so you got rid of it. But I'm saying that proportional representation by race is not guaranteed for the country. Yes. The communists got elected every time. I didn't quite understand you, Mr. Justice. In New York, the communists got elected every time. In Cincinnati, I got elected. You know, I thought, in working on this case, really, one of the most interesting things was the footnote that Mr. Justice White wrote in Whitcomb v. Chavez, where he pointed out that a white man won in a black war, and a black man won in a white war. And I hope that I have lived to see the day where that is America, because if you start carving up cities just because you've got to guarantee black seats on the governing board, you're going to have to carve up northbound cities. Mr. Blackcher. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. I would like to begin by responding, if I may, to some of the questions concerning the commission form of government in Mobile. Briefly, the history of commission government in Mobile, as Mr. Justice Stewart pointed out, began in 1911. The original statute did not require, but did authorize, the commissioners, once they were elected, to divide up the executive functions among themselves. And it certainly was the practice and custom in Mobile almost from the beginning for the commissioners to do this. In fact, it is not a matter of record in this case, but there was a lawsuit in the 1920s by some politicians who were unhappy that the commission had adopted that course, rather than acting as a board of directors in common. You mean that after their election, they then decided which of them was to take what to first? That's correct. And in 1939, it's further my understanding, that the law was explicitly changed to provide for one place to be the mayor in advance of the election, and the two associate commissioners would be assigned executive functions after the election. That plan also ran into some technical problems in the Alabama state courts, and it ended up in 1965. For the first time, the executive functions of the three commissioners were designated by law before they ran. Again, we would like to point out that the plaintiffs in this case never objected to the retention of a commission form of government which permitted the use of single-member districts. It was the position of the defendant's city in this case. From the time it filed its answer, through its arguments in the pretrial motions, the pretrial document, pretrial briefs, and on into the Court of Appeals, that the assignment of executive functions to the three commissioners foreclosed, absolutely foreclosed, any remedy in this case. That, in fact, was, I think, a keystone of their defense. Based on their representations, which can also be found, by the way, in their answer on page 33 of the appendix, that in order for single-member districts to be provided in Mobile, a change in the form of government would have to come about, the Court acting in its equitable discretion when it was forced to enter an order of its own, when the city of Mobile and the state of Alabama refused, after the Court's invitation, to supply some legislative response to the infirmities of the at-large election system. Then the Court, taking the advice of the defendants themselves, changed to an optional form of government which is provided in the state of Alabama by other statutes. The state of Alabama has several optional forms of municipal government, including the now ancient mayor-alternatic form of government which Mobile was using back in 1900, including a newer mayor council form that was devised specifically for Mobile in 1963, and including special legislation that governs Montgomery, for example, and Birmingham, which have adopted the so-called strong mayor that everyone in this trial agreed was preferable to the wheat mayor, where the council could interfere in the day-to-day business of the executive. But to repeat, it is true that the plaintiffs, in the end, when asked to propose a remedy, suggested a change to a mayor council only because the defendants were urging that any other use of a form of government in the context of single-member districts would be inequitable and inappropriate and mobile. The Court's remedy leaves open to the state of Alabama the option of adopting by legislation a commissioned form of government that does permit of the use of single-member districts. That is still open to Alabama if it wishes to use it. But there has been no movement on the part of anyone in the legislature or in city government to seek or to bring about such a change. Could the city do it unilaterally, or does it take state legislative action? The city took the position from the beginning that it lacked, entirely lacked, any authority to change its election system or its form of government, and that, in fact, we had to look to the legislature of Alabama for our remedy. And he filed a motion to strike. Our prayer for relief that the election system be changed to single-member districts because they lacked the authority to provide that relief. Well, is it your position that the discrimination in this case was effected in the voting booth? Is that where the... Not exactly, Mr. Justice White. We do not take the position that voters are somehow practicing a prohibited, constitutionally prohibited form of discrimination when they vote along racial lines. What our position is that given that situation, a situation, by the way, which has been reinforced by 100 years of official state action... A city should not provide the kind of a system that makes effective that kind of voting, is that it? That's absolutely correct. In Mobile, I doubt that one could devise an electoral form that more carefully and distinctly focused the electoral power of this election. At-large voting is just, in a city, say, is out, is unconstitutional if, over a period of time, a substantial black or some other minority group is without representation. And that the court finds that there's discriminatory voting. Polarized voting. We do not even say that every at-large system, under those circumstances, would have the prescribed effect. After all, as someone here pointed out, there were, in a true at-large system, in a true at-large system, as in this case, the top three vote-getters would be elected. And you could have plurality victories. And it may have been that under such a system, blacks in Mobile, representing 33 percent of the population, would have had the clout to do it. What would you do in this case if blacks and whites had been equally distributed throughout the city? What would have been your remedy? Mr. Justice White, you're correct that we would have had no remedy through the districting formula. And in the first instance, we think that it's unrealistic to consider such a possibility, since if, in fact, blacks and whites were residentially homogenized throughout the entire district, it is unlikely that the social phenomenon of polarized racial voting would have occurred in the first instance. But if it did occur in that circumstance, I think it's clear that the election form, at-large voting, would not be the specific cause of the dilution of their vote. Because, as you say, changing the districts would not provide them such a remedy. That issue, of course, is not presented here. The evidence was, and the court found, that Mobile was one of the most racially segregated cities in the country. What inferences should be drawn, if any, from the fact that if you'd had district representation here, the three Negro candidates who ran would not have been elected in their own predominantly Negro districts? Yes, sir. That was a factual issue that was debated at great length in the trial court. And all of the facts indicated, and the trial court found, and the Court of Appeals affirmed its finding, that it was an indication that no well-known, well-financed black candidate was even going to attempt a race in the city of Mobile, where all of the politicians, including the defendants, conceded that it took $30,000 to $50,000 to wage a successful campaign. When all of the black politicians, including the floor, nonpartisan voters' league, represented to the court that they would not even attempt to launch a black candidate, given the pattern of racially polarized voting. This was a situation where the one champion of blacks' interests in the city of Mobile, a white commissioner named Joe Langan, had been defeated by that same racially polarized voting. His situation provided the centerpiece, I think, of the evidence in this case. And blacks in this case did not contend that they had a right to have a districting remedy that would permit them to elect blacks. They wished to elect a candidate of their choice. They weren't, the evidence indicated they were not even permitted by the white majority to elect a white candidate who was at all connected with or interested in their concerns. How were they prevented from doing it? I beg your pardon, Mr. Johnson. You said the Negroes weren't allowed to elect the man of their own choice. And my question was, how were they denied that right? They were denied that right by the block voting white majority operating in an at-large election system that involved a majority vote requirement. Well, I understand from Mr. Ryan that maybe you can help him. He wants to know the constitutional provision that prevents white people from voting for white people and Negro and black people from voting for black people. There is no such constitutional provision in the police court. I agree with you on that. We certainly do. Always have.
